tests.title: English Language & Comprehension Practice — Error Spotting & Improvement
tests.subject: Computer Science
tests.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Despite of the heavy rain / the match / was played / as scheduled.
questions.explanation_en: “Despite” is never followed by “of”. Correct: Despite the heavy rain (or In spite of the heavy rain).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
She told me / that she / didn’t knew / the answer.
questions.explanation_en: After “did/didn’t”, the main verb takes its base form: didn’t know.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
The furniture in the new office / are made / of teak wood / and looks elegant.

options.en: The furniture in the new office

questions.explanation_en: “Furniture” is an uncountable, singular noun, so the verb should be “is made”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error. If there is no error, select option 4.
He is taller / than any other boy / in his class.
questions.explanation_en: The comparative with “any other + singular noun” is correct, so the sentence has no error.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
I have been knowing / him since / we were children / in the same school.
questions.explanation_en: “Know” is a stative verb and is not used in continuous tenses. Correct: I have known him since ...

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Hardly had he reached / the station / than the train / left without him.
questions.explanation_en: “Hardly” is followed by “when”, not “than” (“No sooner” takes “than”).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Rahul is one of the boys / who has / won medals / in the national games.

options.en: Rahul is one of the boys

questions.explanation_en: In “one of the + plural noun + who”, the relative pronoun refers to the plural noun, so the verb is “have”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
She gave me / a very good advices / on how to / prepare for the interview.
questions.explanation_en: “Advice” is uncountable and has no plural form. Correct: a piece of advice / very good advice.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
The Principal, along with / the teachers, / are planning / a farewell party.
questions.explanation_en: The subject “Principal” is singular; “along with” does not make it plural. Use “is planning”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Between you and I, / the project / is not likely / to succeed.
questions.explanation_en: A preposition takes the objective case: “Between you and me”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error. If there is no error, select option 4.
The book that / I bought yesterday / is very interesting.
questions.explanation_en: The sentence is grammatically correct; the relative clause and verb agree properly.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
My uncle / is working / in this company / since 2010.
questions.explanation_en: “Since 2010” needs the present perfect continuous: has been working.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Though he was tired, / but he / continued working / on the project.
questions.explanation_en: “Though” and “but” should not be used together in one sentence. Remove “but”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
I prefer / walking than / driving to / the office.
questions.explanation_en: “Prefer” takes “to”: I prefer walking to driving.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
She [hardly never] visits her native village.
questions.explanation_en: “Hardly” already has a negative sense, so “never” cannot be added. The correct idiom is “hardly ever”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
I [am living] in Jaipur since my childhood.
questions.explanation_en: “Since + point of time” with an action continuing now needs the present perfect continuous: have been living.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
The teacher asked the boy [why was he late].
questions.explanation_en: In reported questions the word order becomes that of a statement (subject before verb): why he was late.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
He suggested [me to take] a taxi.
questions.explanation_en: “Suggest” is not followed by an object + to-infinitive. It takes a that-clause (that I take / that I should take) or a gerund.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
Each of the girls [have] brought her own lunch.
questions.explanation_en: “Each” is singular and needs “has”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
The cost of living [have risen] sharply this year.
questions.explanation_en: The subject “cost” is singular, so the verb must be “has risen”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
I would have helped you [if you would have asked].
questions.explanation_en: In the third conditional, the if-clause uses the past perfect (if + had + V3) and the main clause uses would have + V3.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
She is [more taller] than her sister.
questions.explanation_en: A one-syllable adjective forms the comparative with -er; “more” must not be added (double comparative).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
He [is knowing] the answer to every question.
questions.explanation_en: “Know” is a stative verb and is not used in continuous forms; use the simple present.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
Neither the teacher [or the students] were aware of the changes.
questions.explanation_en: “Neither” is paired with “nor”, not “or”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
Scarcely had I reached the gate [than the bell rang].
questions.explanation_en: 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' are paired with 'when' (or 'before'); only 'No sooner' takes 'than'. So the correct form is 'Scarcely had I reached the gate when the bell rang'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
[Not only he is] a good singer but also a fine dancer.
questions.explanation_en: When a sentence begins with 'Not only', the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion): 'Not only is he a good singer but also a fine dancer'. 'Does he' would need a main verb such as 'sing'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
He has been / absent in the class / for the last / three days.
questions.explanation_en: The adjective 'absent' takes 'from': 'absent from the class'. The other segments are correct.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
She looked / very much / beautiful / in the red saree.
questions.explanation_en: 'Very' modifies an adjective in the positive degree (very beautiful); 'much' is used with comparatives and past participles (much better, much admired). So 'very much beautiful' is wrong.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The scenery / of Kashmir / are very / charming in spring.
questions.explanation_en: 'Scenery' is an uncountable noun and is always singular, so the verb must be 'is very charming'. Similar nouns: furniture, luggage, information, advice.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
If he will come / tomorrow, / I shall discuss / the matter with him.
questions.explanation_en: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the simple present even for a future idea: 'If he comes tomorrow, I shall discuss...'. 'Will' belongs only in the main clause.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
He returned back / from Mumbai / late last night / by the express train.
questions.explanation_en: 'Return' already means 'come back', so 'returned back' is redundant. Similar errors: repeat again, revert back, cousin brother.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
The jury were divided / in their opinions / about the verdict.
questions.explanation_en: A collective noun takes a plural verb when its members act as individuals with different views. 'The jury were divided in their opinions' is correct; 'their' confirms the plural sense.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The doctor [wrote] a strong medicine for the patient's fever.
questions.explanation_en: A doctor 'prescribes' medicine; 'prescribe' is the exact word for recommending a treatment. 'Described' means told about and 'subscribed' means paid for regularly.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The Principal [laid stress over] the need for discipline in the morning assembly.
questions.explanation_en: The fixed expression is 'lay stress on' (also 'lay emphasis on', 'insist on'). 'Over', 'at' and 'for' are not used with 'stress' in this sense.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
She [has been working] in this school for ten years and still loves her job.
questions.explanation_en: 'For ten years' with an action that continues now ('still loves her job') needs the present perfect continuous, which is already used. So no substitution is required.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The clever thief managed to ______ the police for a whole week.
questions.explanation_en: 'Elude' means to escape or avoid being caught. 'Allude' means to refer indirectly, 'collude' to conspire secretly and 'exclude' to leave out.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to BENEVOLENT.
questions.explanation_en: Benevolent means well-meaning and kindly.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
questions.explanation_en: Candid means truthful and straightforward, i.e. frank.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to OBSOLETE.
questions.explanation_en: Obsolete describes something no longer in use or out of date.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to METICULOUS.
questions.explanation_en: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail; painstaking is the nearest synonym.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to EPHEMERAL.
questions.explanation_en: Ephemeral things last for a very short time.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to ABATE.
questions.explanation_en: To abate is to become less intense, e.g. the storm abated; subside is closest.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to ARDENT.
questions.explanation_en: Ardent means enthusiastic and passionate.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to FRUGAL.
questions.explanation_en: Frugal means careful about spending money, i.e. thrifty.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to PERNICIOUS.
questions.explanation_en: Pernicious means having a gradual but destructive, harmful effect.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to CAPRICIOUS.
questions.explanation_en: Capricious means given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour, i.e. fickle.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to SAGACIOUS.
questions.explanation_en: Sagacious means having sound judgement; wise is its synonym.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to TENACIOUS.
questions.explanation_en: Tenacious means holding firmly to a purpose; persistent is nearest.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to GENEROUS.
questions.explanation_en: Generous means giving freely; its antonym is stingy (unwilling to give).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to SCARCE.
questions.explanation_en: Scarce means in short supply; abundant means plentiful.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to EXPAND.
questions.explanation_en: Expand means to become larger; contract means to become smaller.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to AMATEUR.
questions.explanation_en: An amateur is non-professional; the opposite is professional.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to VERBOSE.
questions.explanation_en: Verbose means using more words than needed; concise means brief and to the point.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to TRANSPARENT.
questions.explanation_en: Transparent allows light to pass through; opaque does not.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to DILIGENT.
questions.explanation_en: Diligent means hard-working; indolent means habitually lazy.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to BENIGN.
questions.explanation_en: Benign means harmless or gentle; malignant means harmful or disease-causing (e.g. a malignant tumour).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to INEVITABLE.
questions.explanation_en: Inevitable means unable to be avoided; avoidable is its opposite.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to ZENITH.
questions.explanation_en: Zenith is the highest point; nadir is the lowest point.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to TACITURN.
questions.explanation_en: Taciturn means habitually silent; talkative is its antonym.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to MAGNANIMOUS.
questions.explanation_en: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving; petty means small-minded and mean.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘That which cannot be read’.
questions.explanation_en: Illegible means impossible to read because of poor handwriting or print; illiterate refers to a person who cannot read.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘That which cannot be avoided’.
questions.explanation_en: Inevitable means certain to happen and unavoidable.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘One who devotes his life to the welfare of others’.
questions.explanation_en: An altruist is selflessly concerned for the well-being of others; an egoist is self-centred.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘Government by a small group of people’.
questions.explanation_en: Oligarchy = rule by a few; democracy = by the people; monarchy/autocracy = by one.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘The scientific study of birds’.
questions.explanation_en: Ornithology is the study of birds; entomology is of insects, etymology of word origins.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘One who knows everything’.
questions.explanation_en: Omniscient = all-knowing; omnipotent = all-powerful; omnipresent = present everywhere.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘A place where bees are kept’.
questions.explanation_en: An apiary houses bees; an aviary houses birds.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘The killing of a king’.
questions.explanation_en: Regicide (Latin rex = king) is the killing of a king; fratricide is killing of a brother.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘An abnormal fear of open or crowded places’.
questions.explanation_en: Agoraphobia is fear of open spaces; claustrophobia is fear of closed spaces.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘A person who hates mankind’.
questions.explanation_en: A misanthrope hates or distrusts people in general; a misogynist hates women.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘To break the ice’.

options.en: To start a conversation in a social setting

questions.explanation_en: “Break the ice” means to ease the initial awkwardness between people who have just met.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘Once in a blue moon’.
questions.explanation_en: “Once in a blue moon” means something that happens extremely rarely.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
The ______ shop sells pens and paper, but the bus outside remained ______ for an hour.

questions.question_en:
Passage: Water is (1) ______ for all living beings. However, in recent years many cities have been (2) ______ from acute water shortage. The main reason is the (3) ______ use of groundwater by industries and households. If we do not take steps to (4) ______ water, future generations will have to pay a heavy price. Every citizen should therefore (5) ______ responsibility and avoid wastage.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (1).
Relevant sentence: Water is (1) ______ for all living beings.
questions.explanation_en: Water is necessary for all life, so “essential” fits the context.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Sleep is often treated as a luxury by students and working adults, yet scientists consider it as essential as food and water. During sleep the brain does not simply switch off; it sorts the information gathered during the day, stores important memories and clears away harmful chemicals that accumulate while we are awake. Children who sleep for less than eight hours are more likely to have difficulty in concentrating and to show poor results in examinations. Adults who regularly sleep for only five or six hours face a higher risk of heart disease and depression. Experts therefore advise a fixed bedtime, avoiding screens an hour before sleeping and keeping the bedroom dark and quiet. Contrary to popular belief, sleeping late on weekends cannot fully repay the “sleep debt” collected during the week.

What is the main idea of the passage?

options.en: Weekends are meant for rest only.
Sleep is essential for health and learning.

questions.explanation_en: The passage opens by calling sleep as essential as food and water, then describes its effects on the brain, children and adults.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Trees in cities do much more than make streets look pleasant. A single mature tree can absorb about twenty kilograms of carbon dioxide in a year and release enough oxygen for two people. Their leaves trap dust, while their shade can lower the temperature of a neighbourhood by several degrees, reducing the need for air conditioners. In many Indian cities, however, trees are felled for widening roads and constructing flyovers, often without any plan to replace them. Urban planners argue that development and greenery are not enemies; roads can be designed around existing trees, and every felled tree can be compensated by planting several saplings. Citizens, too, must take the initiative by protecting trees in their own colony instead of waiting for the government to act.

What is the central theme of the passage?

options.en: Roads are more important than trees.
Urban trees are valuable and should be protected.

questions.explanation_en: The passage details the benefits of city trees and urges planners and citizens to protect them.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
P. Within a few years, the small shop had grown into the largest bookstore in the town.
Q. Ramesh opened a tiny bookshop near the bus stand in 1998 with borrowed money.
R. At first very few customers came, and he often sat alone among the shelves.
S. Slowly, students began to visit because he let them read books free of cost in the shop.
questions.explanation_en: Q introduces Ramesh and the shop, R describes the slow start ('At first'), S the change ('Slowly, students began to visit') and P the result 'within a few years'. Hence QRSP.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Plastic bags take hundreds of years to break down.
B. As a result, they choke drains, harm animals and pollute the soil.
C. Many states have therefore banned single-use plastic bags.
D. Yet millions of them are thrown away every day after a single use.
questions.explanation_en: A states the fact, D adds the contrast with 'Yet' (they are still thrown away daily), B gives the result of that ('As a result, they choke drains'), and C the remedy ('therefore banned'). Hence ADBC.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
1) It was then that he decided to become a doctor and serve the poor.
2) When Arun was ten, his grandfather fell seriously ill in their village.
3) The nearest hospital was forty kilometres away, and the old man died on the way.
4) Today he runs a free clinic in the same village.
questions.explanation_en: 2 sets the scene (grandfather's illness), 3 tells what happened, 1 gives the decision ('It was then') which needs 3 before it, and 4 ends in the present ('Today'). Hence 2, 3, 1, 4.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles

Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
P. In the Middle Ages books were copied by hand, so only the rich could own them.
Q. The invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century changed this.
R. As a result, knowledge, once the property of a few, reached ordinary people.
S. Books could now be produced quickly and sold cheaply.
questions.explanation_en: P gives the old situation, Q the change ('changed this' refers back to P), S the immediate effect of printing ('could now be produced quickly') and R the wider result ('As a result'). Hence PQSR.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in the correct order.
The government has decided
P. so that no child
Q. in remote villages
R. is left without education
S. to open new schools
questions.explanation_en: 'Decided' is followed by the infinitive S 'to open new schools', then Q 'in remote villages', then the purpose clause P 'so that no child' and R 'is left without education'. Hence SQPR.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

What is the main idea of the passage?

options.en: Rice and wheat are more nutritious than millets.
Millets declined after the Green Revolution and are now being revived.
The Green Revolution was a complete failure.
Millets can be grown only in rain-fed areas.

questions.explanation_en: The passage traces millets from staple food, to decline after the Green Revolution, to the recent revival (International Year of Millets, school meals). The other options are either not stated or contradicted.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

According to the passage, why are millets well suited to India?

options.en: They give the highest yield of all cereals.
They grow on poor soil with very little water.
They are easy to export to other countries.

questions.explanation_en: The passage says millets 'grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures', which suits a country where most farmland depends on rain.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of millets?

options.en: They are rich in iron and calcium.
They are rich in vitamin C.

questions.explanation_en: Fibre, iron, calcium and the slow release of sugar (helping diabetes) are all mentioned. Vitamin C is never mentioned, so option 4 is the answer.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

Select the word closest in meaning to 'staple' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation_en: 'Staple food' is the main or basic food eaten regularly by a people. Rare, costly and seasonal do not fit 'the staple food of most Indian households'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

What can be inferred from the warning given by nutrition experts?

options.en: Millets will soon replace rice and wheat completely.
Farmers' earnings will decide whether the millet revival lasts.
School meals should stop serving millet dishes.
The United Nations will pay farmers to grow millets.

questions.explanation_en: The experts say the revival 'will last only if farmers receive a fair price'. So its future depends on farmers' income; the other options are not supported by the text.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: When Meena Devi was posted to a government school in a small hill village, the building had two rooms, a leaking roof and forty children who came only on days when there was no work in the fields. Instead of complaining, she began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents, learnt the local dialect and explained, without lecturing, why reading mattered. She turned the school veranda into a library with old newspapers and picture books collected from friends in the city. Within two years attendance had nearly doubled, and the village panchayat, moved by her persistence, repaired the roof with its own funds. Meena Devi never claimed the credit. 'The children did the work,' she said when a journalist asked about her success. 'I only kept the door open.'

Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.en: The Teacher Who Kept the Door Open

questions.explanation_en: The passage is about how Meena Devi transformed a village school, and it ends with her line 'I only kept the door open'. The other titles cover only a detail.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: When Meena Devi was posted to a government school in a small hill village, the building had two rooms, a leaking roof and forty children who came only on days when there was no work in the fields. Instead of complaining, she began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents, learnt the local dialect and explained, without lecturing, why reading mattered. She turned the school veranda into a library with old newspapers and picture books collected from friends in the city. Within two years attendance had nearly doubled, and the village panchayat, moved by her persistence, repaired the roof with its own funds. Meena Devi never claimed the credit. 'The children did the work,' she said when a journalist asked about her success. 'I only kept the door open.'

How did Meena Devi begin her effort to improve the school?

options.en: By punishing children who stayed away
By visiting families and listening to parents
By asking the panchayat for funds
By writing to newspapers in the city

questions.explanation_en: 'She began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents...'. The panchayat repaired the roof later, on its own, and she never wrote to newspapers.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: When Meena Devi was posted to a government school in a small hill village, the building had two rooms, a leaking roof and forty children who came only on days when there was no work in the fields. Instead of complaining, she began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents, learnt the local dialect and explained, without lecturing, why reading mattered. She turned the school veranda into a library with old newspapers and picture books collected from friends in the city. Within two years attendance had nearly doubled, and the village panchayat, moved by her persistence, repaired the roof with its own funds. Meena Devi never claimed the credit. 'The children did the work,' she said when a journalist asked about her success. 'I only kept the door open.'

Select the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'persistence' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation_en: 'Persistence' means continuing firmly despite difficulty. Its opposite is 'irresolution' (lack of firmness, wavering). Perseverance, determination and endurance are near-synonyms.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: When Meena Devi was posted to a government school in a small hill village, the building had two rooms, a leaking roof and forty children who came only on days when there was no work in the fields. Instead of complaining, she began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents, learnt the local dialect and explained, without lecturing, why reading mattered. She turned the school veranda into a library with old newspapers and picture books collected from friends in the city. Within two years attendance had nearly doubled, and the village panchayat, moved by her persistence, repaired the roof with its own funds. Meena Devi never claimed the credit. 'The children did the work,' she said when a journalist asked about her success. 'I only kept the door open.'

What does Meena Devi's reply to the journalist show about her?

options.en: She was proud of her fame.
She wanted a transfer to the city.
She was modest and gave the credit to others.

questions.explanation_en: 'Meena Devi never claimed the credit' and she said 'The children did the work'. This shows modesty, not pride or dislike.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: When Meena Devi was posted to a government school in a small hill village, the building had two rooms, a leaking roof and forty children who came only on days when there was no work in the fields. Instead of complaining, she began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents, learnt the local dialect and explained, without lecturing, why reading mattered. She turned the school veranda into a library with old newspapers and picture books collected from friends in the city. Within two years attendance had nearly doubled, and the village panchayat, moved by her persistence, repaired the roof with its own funds. Meena Devi never claimed the credit. 'The children did the work,' she said when a journalist asked about her success. 'I only kept the door open.'

What does Meena Devi most likely mean by 'I only kept the door open'?

options.en: She only gave the children the opportunity to learn.
She guarded the school building at night.
She never locked the classroom door.
She allowed parents to visit at any time.

questions.explanation_en: The line is figurative: she created the chance (an open door) and the children used it themselves. The literal readings about doors and locks miss the point.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (1).
Relevant sentence: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field.
questions.explanation_en: Discipline is presented as the base on which success is built, so 'foundation' fits. 'Enemy' contradicts the passage and 'ceiling' and 'result' make no sense here.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (2).
Relevant sentence: A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus...
questions.explanation_en: Only a student who follows a timetable would find it easier to finish the syllabus; the other three verbs reverse the meaning.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (3).
Relevant sentence: ...finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination.
questions.explanation_en: 'Well before the examination' means comfortably ahead of it, which is the advantage of discipline. 'After' and 'during' are illogical and 'since' needs a past starting point.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (4).
Relevant sentence: Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment.
questions.explanation_en: The fixed phrase is 'live in fear of' something. 'Under', 'with' and 'from' do not combine with 'fear of' in this sense.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (5).
Relevant sentence: Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.
questions.explanation_en: 'Seldom' is negative in meaning, so the verb must describe failure: disciplined people 'seldom miss their goals'. 'Seldom reach/achieve/set' would say the opposite of the passage.

tests.title: English Language & Comprehension — 200 Most Expected Questions (Full Test)
