questions.question_en: Select the option that contains no spelling error.

options.en: The horrizontal movements of ocean water are refferred to as currents, while the vertical changes are called upwelling or downwelling.
The horizontal movements of ocean water are refered to as currents, while the vertical changes are called upwelling or downwelling.
The horizontal movements of ocean water are referred to as currents, while the vertical changes are called upwelling or downwelling.
The horrizontal movements of ocean water are referred to as currents, while the vertical changes are called upwelling or downwelling.

questions.explanation_en: 'Horizontal' has a single r and 'referred' doubles the r before -ed because the stress falls on the final syllable (re-FER). Only option 3 spells both words correctly; the others contain 'horrizontal', 'refferred' or 'refered'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given proverb.
You can't have your cake and eat it too

options.en: Not to worry much about trivial matters
Encourage people to achieve at least one goal, if not two
To do two things that are similar to each other
Unable to do two things that are contradictory to each other

questions.explanation_en: 'You can't have your cake and eat it too' means you cannot enjoy two mutually contradictory advantages at once - once the cake is eaten, you no longer have it. Hence option 4, being unable to do two contradictory things, is the correct meaning.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
1) Travellers should, however, realise that change cannot be brought by a single person, and we should join hands together and vow to follow the traffic rules.
2) Eight out of ten road accidents are caused by the people who don't follow the rules of the road.
3) Abiding by the traffic rules will only help us in having a smooth traffic flow and preventing road accidents.
4) Road safety rules are meant for public safety and to keep the traffic congestion in check.
questions.explanation_en: Sentence 4 introduces the topic (road safety rules), 2 gives the statistic on rule-breakers causing accidents, 1 adds 'however' that change needs collective effort, and 3 concludes with the benefit of following rules. So the order 4-2-1-3 (option 3) is coherent.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word/ set of given words.
Garima has a propensity for being the attention seeker in the department.
She's inherited from her father a propensity to talk too much
questions.explanation_en: 'Propensity' means a natural tendency or inclination to behave in a certain way. Its opposite is 'disinclination' (unwillingness); aptness and disposition are near-synonyms and competence is unrelated.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who believes in ruthless self-aggrandisement
questions.explanation_en: An egoist is a self-centred person who pursues his own interest and self-aggrandisement (enlarging his own power or importance). An altruist is the opposite, an introvert is shy, and an iconoclast attacks established beliefs, so 'Egoist' fits.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The ideal detect dog / is extremely energetic / with an excessive / play drive.
questions.explanation_en: A noun used as a modifier here must be 'detection', not the verb 'detect': the correct phrase is 'The ideal detection dog'. The other segments ('is extremely energetic', 'with an excessive play drive') are grammatical, so segment 1 has the error.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
Barely has they won the match when the coach had a heart attack.
questions.explanation_en: 'Barely/Hardly/Scarcely ... when' expresses one past action immediately followed by another, so it takes the past perfect with inversion: 'Barely had they won the match when...'. 'Has' is wrong for a past context and 'did ... won' is ungrammatical, so option 4 is correct.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The sparrows are / some of the few birds / that engage on / dust bathing.
questions.explanation_en: The verb 'engage' takes the preposition 'in' when it means to take part in an activity: 'engage in dust bathing'. 'Engage on' is incorrect, so segment 4 contains the error.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank with the correct collocation.
If you read _____ you will clearly see what he means.
questions.explanation_en: 'Read between the lines' is a fixed collocation meaning to understand the hidden or implied meaning. The other prepositions do not form this idiom, so option 4 is correct.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the option that contains no spelling error.

options.en: Conservation canines are fast becoming indispensable tools for biologists.
Conservation cannines are fast becoming indispensible tools for biologicsts.
Conversatoin canines are fast becoming indispensable tools for biologists.
Conversation canines are fast becoming indespensible tools for biologists.

questions.explanation_en: The correct spellings are 'conservation', 'canines', 'indispensable' and 'biologists'. Only option 1 has all of them correct; the others contain 'cannines', 'indispensible', 'biologicsts', 'conversatoin' or 'indespensible'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
No sooner had the company launch its new product than it went bankrupt.

options.en: No sooner had the company launched
No sooner did the company launched
No sooner have the company launched

questions.explanation_en: 'No sooner ... than' is followed by the past perfect with subject-auxiliary inversion: 'No sooner had + subject + V3'. So 'had the company launch' must become 'had the company launched' (option 2); 'did ... launched' and 'have the company' are ungrammatical.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Blow off steam

options.en: To get rid of pent-up energy or strong emotion

questions.explanation_en: 'Blow off steam' means to release pent-up energy or strong emotions such as anger, often through activity. Option 2 states exactly this idiomatic sense.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
1) As one starts growing old, the lens of the eye hardens, loses its transparency and becomes opaque.
2) Cataract is the major cause of blindness, which is also caused by a damage to the cornea.
3) It obstructs the light rays from entering the eye.
4) It occurs more often in old age.
questions.explanation_en: Sentence 2 introduces cataract as a major cause of blindness, 4 says it occurs more often in old age, 1 explains that the eye lens hardens and becomes opaque with ageing, and 3 says this blocks light rays. Hence 2-4-1-3 (option 2).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Study of various aspects of aging
questions.explanation_en: Gerontology is the scientific study of ageing and of the problems of old people (Greek geron = old man). Chronology is the order of events, genealogy the study of family lineage, and microbiology the study of microbes.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate homonym to fill in the blanks.
As she _____ her hands from the deck I fear the huge _____ of ocean.
questions.explanation_en: 'Waves' fits both blanks with different meanings: 'she waves her hands' (verb: moves in greeting) and 'the huge waves of ocean' (noun: moving ridges of water). The other words do not suit both blanks.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Comprehension:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

When I was very little, I caught the travel bug. It started after my grandparents first brought me to their home in France and I have now been to twenty-nine different countries. Each has given me a unique learning experience.

At five, I marvelled at the Eiffel Tower in the City of Lights. When I was eight, I stood in the heart of Piazza San Marco feeding hordes of pigeons, then glided down Venetian waterways on sleek gondolas. At thirteen, I saw the ancient, megalithic structure of Stonehenge and walked along the Great Wall of China, amazed that the thousand-year-old stones were still in place.

It was through exploring cultures around the world that I first became interested in language.

It began with French, which taught me the importance of pronunciation. I remember once asking a store owner in Paris where Rue des Pyramides was. But when I pronounced it PYR–a–mides instead of pyr–A–mides, with more accent on the A, she looked at me bewildered.

In the eighth grade, I became fascinated with Spanish and aware of its similarities with English through cognates. Baseball in Spanish, for example, is béisbol, which looks different but sounds nearly the same. This was incredible to me as it made speech and comprehension more fluid, and even today I find that cognates come to the rescue when I forget how to say something in Spanish.

I loved how long words were formed by combining simpler characters, so Huǒ meaning fire and Shān meaning mountain can be joined to create Huǒshān, which means volcano. I love spending hours at a time practicing the characters and I can feel the beauty and rhythm as I form them.

Identify the tone of the given passage.
questions.explanation_en: The writer narrates personal experiences in chronological order and describes places and languages in detail, without sadness or pretence. Hence the tone is narrative and descriptive (option 3).

questions.question_en:
Comprehension:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

When I was very little, I caught the travel bug. It started after my grandparents first brought me to their home in France and I have now been to twenty-nine different countries. Each has given me a unique learning experience.

It was through exploring cultures around the world that I first became interested in language.

It began with French, which taught me the importance of pronunciation. I remember once asking a store owner in Paris where Rue des Pyramides was. But when I pronounced it PYR–a–mides instead of pyr–A–mides, with more accent on the A, she looked at me bewildered.

Baseball in Spanish, for example, is béisbol, which looks different but sounds nearly the same. Then, in high school, I developed an enthusiasm for Chinese. As I studied Chinese at my school, I marvelled how if just one stroke was missing from a character, the meaning is lost. I love spending hours at a time practicing the characters and I can feel the beauty and rhythm as I form them.

SubQuestion No : 17
Identify the most suitable title for the given passage.
questions.explanation_en: The passage links the author's travels to the growth of his interest in French, Spanish and Chinese. 'Travel and Language' captures both themes, while the other titles cover only a part or are unrelated.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Predictable
questions.explanation_en: 'Predictable' means able to be foreseen or expected. Its opposite is 'improbable' (unlikely to happen); foreseeable, certain and expected are all close in meaning to predictable.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Miss the boat
questions.explanation_en: 'Miss the boat' means to lose an opportunity by being too slow to act. It has nothing to do with literal boat travel, so option 1, 'miss a chance', is correct.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.Two IAF MiG fighters from the Adampur base crashed following a mid-air collision.
B.As a result, a fire broke out in four houses, and four boys playing in a field were wounded when the debris fell on them.
C.The other fighter plane crashed in the fields of Chansu Jattan.
D.According to reports, one plane crashed near Pensara.
questions.explanation_en: A introduces the crash of two MiG fighters, D reports where one plane crashed, C follows with 'the other fighter plane', and B describes the result (fire and injuries). So ADCB is the logical order.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
It is so refreshing to walk through the beach early in the morning.
questions.explanation_en: We walk 'along' or 'on' a beach, i.e. over its surface; 'through' implies moving inside something enclosed like a forest or tunnel. Hence 'through the beach' contains the error.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.
A collection of weapons and military equipment
questions.explanation_en: An arsenal is a collection or store of weapons and military equipment. An archive stores records, an apiary is a place for keeping bees, and an asylum is a place of refuge.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
My injured _____ will _____ soon.
questions.explanation_en: 'Heel' (noun) is the back part of the foot and 'heal' (verb) means to become healthy again. The sentence needs a noun first and a verb after 'will', so 'heel; heal' (option 3).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.We can request the public library to send us all the books that they will be replacing this year.
B.However, I think, I have solution to this problem.
C.That means, no books till the next academic session.
D.Yesterday I was told that we had exhausted our library funds for this year.
questions.explanation_en: D states the problem (library funds exhausted), C gives its consequence (no books till next session), B introduces a solution with 'However', and A states the solution. Hence DCBA.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
Post covid, international air travel is hopping back to normalcy.
questions.explanation_en: 'Hopping' suggests lively, energetic movement, which contradicts the slow, struggling recovery of air travel after Covid. 'Limping back to normalcy' is the standard expression for a slow, difficult recovery, so option 1.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Short fuse
questions.explanation_en: A person with a 'short fuse' gets angry very quickly, just as a short fuse makes an explosive go off quickly. Hence option 4.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation_en: 'Crucial' is spelt correctly. The correct forms of the others are 'competence', 'command' and 'complexity'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined phrase in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The Mysore palace is gearing up for the winter festival.
questions.explanation_en: 'Gear up for' means to prepare for an event, which fits the palace preparing for the winter festival. The sentence is already correct, so no substitution is required.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
There is a _____ train from Mysore to Chennai.
questions.explanation_en: The fixed collocation is 'fast train' (as in fast food, fast car). Speedy, brisk and quick are not used idiomatically with 'train' in this sense, so option 4.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.
The study of evolution of mankind
questions.explanation_en: Anthropology is the study of human beings, including the evolution of mankind, their societies and cultures. Geology studies the earth, archaeology studies ancient remains, and cartography is map-making.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Whether I do not agree with her views, I respect her for her honesty.
questions.explanation_en: 'Whether' introduces alternatives or doubt and cannot express contrast. A concessive clause needs 'Though/Although': 'Though I do not agree with her views, I respect her...'. So segment 4 has the error.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
questions.explanation_en: The correct spelling is 'allot' (double l, single t). Associate, attendance and accept are spelt correctly, so 'Alott' is the incorrectly spelt word.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Comprehension:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

“Any bicycle repair shop around? Can anyone share the location please?”
That was a desperate appeal from a woman in our residents’ association’s WhatsApp group. Her child’s bicycle needed urgent mending.
“There is one around 2 km away.” Soon came the first response.
“No. The shop shut long ago, even before COVID,” someone else chipped in.
Where have the bicycle repairers gone? The wayside mechanics who would do a gamut of works on your bicycles for a paltry sum have almost gone extinct. These days, only children use bicycles, and you know a mechanic needs regular customers to survive. There is a time in almost everyone’s life when they become proud owners of their first bicycle. And there comes a stage when we abandon the prized possession and graduate ourselves to a motorised vehicle. Unused and unattended, the bicycles rust and disintegrate and finally end up at scrap dealers.
City roads in Kerala have now become totally unfriendly for bicycles. A cyclist is an odd man out on the chaotic road, an unwelcome disruptor among the automobiles arrogantly jostling for space. There are people out there who love to bicycle to their workplaces but dare not, dreading the reckless traffic on the way.
Is speed synonymous with progress? The transition from bullock carts to bullet trains denotes mankind’s journey toward development. However, passion for speed and more speed could trigger a gasping race to nowhere. To find time to relish the fruits of development, the curve has to slow down and plateau somewhere.
A bicycle is silent like a butterfly, easy like a true friend to possess and maintain. A bicycle symbolises fine balancing, not just on its narrow wheels but a balanced living. This simple carbon-free mode of transport helps the rider to be healthy and heal the habitat. People who cycle to work tend to be less stressed out at workplaces. Motorcyclists whiz past, hiding their heads and thoughts in full-face helmets. Car owners roll up their glasses and cocoon their mind and body from the outside world. A cyclist pedals under the open sky, opens up to friends and fellows on the way and forgets one’s own worries. It seems egalitarianism is part and parcel of the cycling culture.

Q.16 Who is referred to as an ‘unwelcome disrupter’?
questions.explanation_en: The passage says 'A cyclist is an odd man out on the chaotic road, an unwelcome disruptor among the automobiles'. So the cyclist is referred to as the unwelcome disruptor.

options.en: It is an eco-friendly means of transport.
It easily navigates in traffic jams.

questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.

Collins Dictionary picked the word 'permacrisis' as its word of 2022 to describe any widespread period of instability and insecurity.
questions.explanation_en: Collins defined 'permacrisis' as 'an extended period of instability and insecurity'. 'Extended period' is the natural collocation for a long-lasting stretch of time; 'lengthened' and 'elongated' describe physical stretching, so option 4 fits best.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A.This is the story of an unhappy telephone booth that woke up one morning with a headache.
B.A little later a small boy who was watching all this from a distance came and began singing in his lovely voice.
C.A young man came to make a call, but the door wouldn't open; then an old lady came and she also could not open it.
D.And lo and behold! The door opened on its own.
questions.explanation_en: A introduces the story of the unhappy telephone booth, C describes people failing to open its door, B brings in the boy who sang, and D gives the result - the door opened. Hence ACBD.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Break even

options.en: Neither lose nor gain any money

questions.explanation_en: 'Break even' means to reach a point where income equals expenditure, so there is neither profit nor loss. Hence option 2.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I am ______ aware of the consequences of my decision.
questions.explanation_en: 'Fully aware' is the standard collocation meaning completely conscious of something. 'Outrightly' is non-standard, and 'utterly' and 'positively' do not idiomatically pair with 'aware' here.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Please pour the coffee into the flask into the cups.
questions.explanation_en: Coffee is poured 'from' a flask 'into' the cups; the source takes 'from'. So 'into the flask' should be 'from the flask', making option 3 the error.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.

With the coming of rains, people are feeling relieved after the flaming heat of the summer season.
questions.explanation_en: 'Scorching heat' is the standard collocation for intense summer heat. 'Flaming' refers to actual flames, 'ardent' means passionate and 'crackling' is a sound, so option 3 is the best substitute.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
questions.explanation_en: The correct spelling is 'university' with an s. Unison, unpredictable and universal are spelt correctly, so 'Univercity' is incorrect.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation_en: 'Permeate' (to spread through) is correctly spelt. The others should be 'pension', 'persuasion' and 'permission'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.

The arrangement of events or dates in the order of their occurrence
questions.explanation_en: Chronology (chronos = time) is the arrangement of events or dates in the order in which they occurred. Phonology studies speech sounds, geology the earth, and morphology word forms or structures.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A.Louis Braille was born on 4th Jan 1809 in France.
B.Although the doctors did their best, his eyes could not be saved.
C.He had been playing in his father's workshop when the accident took place.
D.When he was 3 years old, Louis lost his eyesight as a result of an accident.
questions.explanation_en: A gives Braille's birth, D says he lost his eyesight at three due to an accident, C explains how the accident happened, and B says doctors could not save his eyes. Hence ADCB.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Liberation
questions.explanation_en: 'Liberation' means setting free. Its opposite is 'subjugation' (bringing under control or domination); emancipation, acquittal and freedom are similar in meaning.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Face the music
questions.explanation_en: 'Face the music' means to accept and confront the unpleasant consequences of one's actions. Hence option 1, 'confront unpleasantness'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.

A large bedroom for a number of people in a school or institution
questions.explanation_en: A dormitory is a large bedroom with many beds for students or members of an institution. A creche is a nursery for infants, a hostel is a whole residential building, and a sanatorium is a place for convalescents.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Fill in the Blanks
questions.question_en:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

I appreciate her being honesty about all her mistakes.
questions.explanation_en: After the gerund 'being', a complement adjective is needed: 'her being honest'. 'Honesty' is a noun and cannot follow 'being' here, so segment 1 is incorrect.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.

Let us ______ at the ______ shop.
questions.explanation_en: 'Meet' (verb) means to come together, and 'meat' (noun) is animal flesh. The sentence needs a verb after 'Let us' and a noun modifier for 'shop', giving 'meet; meat'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Comprehension:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

No matter where you work, sometimes subtle and sometimes very obvious competition is a part and parcel of workplaces. In an environment where most workers are seeking good appraisals, awards, promotions and reputation, fairness is not always on the minds of those competing with each other.
I recall a story in elementary school about how to make a line smaller without cutting it. The answer to the challenge is drawing a bigger line beside the first line so that the one already drawn looks smaller automatically. The moral of the story is that in order to win over others, you don't necessarily need to cut them down. Instead, you can make yourself bigger by being better at the job or earning credibility fairly. Competition is inevitable, but to outshine others, one way is to do a better job or advance yourself by learning and demonstrating skills.
Some people resort to unfair means. They throw colleagues, take credit for others' work, gossip, backbite, go out of their way to please the bosses and do favours outside of work to earn favours at work, etc. When many employees at work take this approach, the culture of the place becomes toxic over time where it is hard for people to trust each other and contribute to a team environment.
Some workers either get frustrated and disengaged and 'quietly quit', that is, they stop caring about work without actually quitting and do the bare minimum to not get fired. Some others simply leave. But quitting is not an option for everyone, especially when their income supports the family. There are extreme scenarios where people have ended their lives or suffered chronic mental or other health problems because they are unable to cope.
Because job hopping is not easy and not always a solution for everyone, changing the toxic culture is important.
A human resources department that truly supports employees and their well-being, a strong leadership and psychological safety at work that allows employees to speak up when they see something wrong without the fear of being reprimanded are some important prerequisites to achieve a work culture that is conducive to equitable growth opportunities for all. Such a work environment would also make the organisation productive.

SubQuestion No : 16
Why does the writer refer to the story from his school days?

options.en: To bring out the power of competitions
To convey that one can win without defeating anyone
To find a clever solution to a problem
To establish the importance of creative thinking

questions.explanation_en: The story shows a line can be made smaller by drawing a bigger one beside it, and the writer states the moral: to win you need not cut others down. So it conveys that one can win without defeating anyone.

Select the option that describes the type of this passage.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Obstinate
questions.explanation_en: 'Obstinate' means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course. 'Headstrong' (self-willed, stubborn) is its synonym; agreeable is nearly the opposite, and devilish and joyful are unrelated.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
Quarantine
questions.explanation_en: To 'quarantine' is to isolate or keep apart, especially to prevent the spread of disease. 'Assimilate' means to absorb or integrate into a group, which is the opposite idea.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate option for the given blank.
You can't hear the chirping of the birds from outside, ______?
questions.explanation_en: A question tag repeats the auxiliary of the main clause with the same subject pronoun and opposite polarity. The main clause 'You can't hear...' is negative with 'can', so the tag is the positive 'can you?'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the sentence with no spelling errors

options.en: Compliance with the traffic laws is neccesary for safe driving.
Compliance with the trafic laws is necessary for safe driving.
Complience with the traffic laws is necessary for safe driving.
Compliance with the traffic laws is necessary for safe driving.

questions.explanation_en: The correct spellings are 'compliance', 'traffic' and 'necessary'. Only option 4 has all three correct; the others contain 'neccesary', 'trafic' or 'complience'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate antonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
We should always be friendly to others and help them in need.
questions.explanation_en: 'Friendly' means kind and pleasant towards others; its opposite is 'hostile' (unfriendly, aggressive). Igneous, scorching and mammoth are unrelated in meaning.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Developing basic
P. is the only way to face an
Q. infrastructure and the production sector
R. responsibility to help states in this respect
S. economic crisis and the Centre has the
questions.explanation_en: 'Developing basic' is followed by Q 'infrastructure and the production sector', then P 'is the only way to face an', S 'economic crisis and the Centre has the', and R 'responsibility to help states'. Hence QPSR.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate idiom for the given situation.
The team stopped working since they had been working for 6 hours continuously.
questions.explanation_en: 'Call it a day' means to stop working on something, usually because one has done enough or is tired. It fits a team stopping after six hours of continuous work.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en: Select the sentence with no spelling errors

options.en: I'd like to rich a consensus on the isue before we take a formal vote.
I'd like to reach a consensus on the essue before we take a formal vote.
I'd like to reach a conssensus on the issue before we take a formal vote.
I'd like to reach a consensus on the issue before we take a formal vote.

questions.explanation_en: The correct forms are 'reach', 'consensus' and 'issue'. Only option 4 spells all of them correctly; the others have 'rich', 'isue', 'essue' or 'conssensus'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
The question below consists of a set of labelled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. As the Plains was settled and grassland converted for crops and grazing, fires were seen as a threat and extinguished.
Q. Historically, fires set by lightning burned naturally at regular intervals across the Great Plains.
R. Native Americans, who saw the benefits, periodically burned the prairie to improve grazing conditions for buffalo.
S. In the last 50 years, as woody plants began increasing and transforming the grassland into a shrub ecosystem, fire has returned to the Plains in the form of controlled burns.
questions.explanation_en: Q gives the historical background (natural lightning fires), R adds that Native Americans also burned the prairie, P describes how settlers began extinguishing fires, and S says fire has returned as controlled burns in the last 50 years. Hence QRPS.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.
He took another bite and chewed ______.
questions.explanation_en: 'Chewed' is a verb, and a verb is modified by an adverb, not an adjective. So the adverb 'slowly' is correct.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.
Nina felt her eyes brim ______ tears and blinked hard.
questions.explanation_en: The verb 'brim' takes the preposition 'with': 'eyes brimmed with tears' means filled to the edge with tears. Hence option 1.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.
The sea provides humanity with a bounty of nutrient-rich food, which we have benefited ______ thousands of years.
questions.explanation_en: The sentence needs a duration expression, 'for thousands of years'. Among the given choices only 'for' is acceptable; 'for since', 'of from' and 'from of' are ungrammatical combinations (ideally the sentence would read 'benefited from for thousands of years').

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.
Melitopol residents ______ the streets following the alleged kidnapping of mayor.
questions.explanation_en: 'Take to the streets' is an idiom meaning to go out into public places to protest. Residents protesting the mayor's kidnapping 'took to the streets'; 'took on' means to accept a challenge.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate option for the given blank.
She was wearing a ball gown in the party, ______?
questions.explanation_en: The main clause 'She was wearing...' is positive with the auxiliary 'was' and subject 'she', so the tag is negative: 'wasn't she?'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, One-word Substitution, Idioms, Spelling
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate idiom for the given situation.
She prepared herself for hard work as her exams were near.
questions.explanation_en: 'Roll up one's sleeves' means to prepare for hard work. 'Drag one's feet' means to delay, and 'back to square one' means to start again, so option 2 fits best.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test & Para Jumbles
questions.question_en:
Comprehension:
Read the following passage and answer the questions given below.
The two main reasons of this chronic and unmanageable problem is rapidly ever increasing population and defective education system. Such a huge population, India finds it difficult to make any significant success in the areas of employment, alleviation of poverty and backwardness. Every sixth person in the world is an Indian. In other words, we are adding an Australia to our population every year or to Japan every ten years. There are about 31 new babies every minute or 45,000 new people daily. Thus, every year there are about 16 million more people to feed, cloth, educate and give employment. This prevailing trend of population growth is quite disturbing.
Unemployment rate in India is showing an increasing trend since 2011 when it was 3.5 percent. The same rose to 3.6 percent in 2012 and climbed to 3.7 percent last year.
Q. Through this passage, the author's main idea is to bring to your notice the ____________.

options.en: population growth of Japan and Australia
low population growth and its benefits
rate of poverty in India and its cause
population explosion in India and the resulting problems

questions.explanation_en: The passage highlights India's rapidly increasing population - figures on births and annual additions - and links it to unemployment, poverty and backwardness. So the main idea is population explosion and its resulting problems.

Read the following passage and answer the questions given below.
The two main reasons of this chronic and unmanageable problem is rapidly ever increasing population and defective education system. Such a huge population, India finds it difficult to make any significant success in the areas of employment, alleviation of poverty and backwardness. Every sixth person in the world is an Indian. In other words, we are adding an Australia to our population every year or to Japan every ten years. There are about 31 new babies every minute or 45,000 new people daily. Thus, every year there are about 16 million more people to feed, cloth, educate and give employment. This prevailing trend of population growth is quite disturbing.
Unemployment rate in India is showing an increasing trend since 2011 when it was 3.5 percent. The same rose to 3.6 percent in 2012 and climbed to 3.7 percent last year.
Q. Which of the following words is opposite in meaning to the word 'extinct' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation_en: 'Extinct' means no longer existing. Its opposite is 'prevailing' (currently existing or widespread), as in 'this prevailing trend'. Lost, obsolete and defunct are synonyms of extinct.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She ______ in Delhi since 2015.
questions.explanation_en: “Since 2015” marks a period continuing up to now, so the present perfect continuous (has been living) is used. Simple past “lived” would mean she no longer lives there.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: By the time the police arrived, the thieves ______.
questions.explanation_en: Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect (had + V3). Escaping happened before the police arrived.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: I ______ the report by tomorrow evening.
questions.explanation_en: “By + future time” shows completion before a future moment, which needs the future perfect (will have + V3).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Look! The children ______ in the garden.
questions.explanation_en: “Look!” signals an action happening at this moment, so the present continuous is required.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: If I ______ you, I would accept the offer.
questions.explanation_en: In an unreal (second) conditional, the if-clause takes the subjunctive “were” for all persons: If I were you, ... would.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The train ______ before we reached the station.
questions.explanation_en: The train’s departure happened earlier than our arrival (both in the past), so the past perfect is used for the earlier action.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The teacher told the class that the earth ______ round the sun.
questions.explanation_en: A universal or scientific truth stays in the simple present even after a past-tense reporting verb.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Hardly ______ the room when the phone rang.
questions.explanation_en: “Hardly/Scarcely/No sooner” is followed by the past perfect, with auxiliary–subject inversion: Hardly had she entered ... when ...

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: I ______ this film three times.
questions.explanation_en: Repeated experience up to the present with no fixed past time takes the present perfect (have seen).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: How long ______ you ______ for the bus?
questions.explanation_en: “How long” with an action that began in the past and continues now takes the present perfect continuous: have you been waiting.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: This time next week, we ______ on the beach in Goa.
questions.explanation_en: “This time next week” refers to an action in progress at a specific future moment, so the future continuous (will be lying) is used.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: He is ______ honest man.
questions.explanation_en: “Honest” begins with a silent h, so it has a vowel sound and takes “an”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: ______ Ganga is the holiest river of India.
questions.explanation_en: Names of rivers take the definite article “the”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She plays ______ guitar very well.
questions.explanation_en: “The” is used before the names of musical instruments when we speak of playing them: play the guitar.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: My brother is studying at ______ university in Pune.
questions.explanation_en: “University” begins with the consonant sound /yu/, so the article is “a”, not “an”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She has ______ MBA degree from a reputed institute.
questions.explanation_en: “MBA” is pronounced “em-bee-ay”, beginning with a vowel sound, so “an” is used.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Rohan goes to ______ school by bus every day.
questions.explanation_en: When a place is visited for its primary purpose (school for studying), no article is used: goes to school.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: What ______ pity that he failed again!
questions.explanation_en: In exclamations with a singular countable noun, “What a/an + noun” is used: What a pity!

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She is ______ European who has settled in Chennai.
questions.explanation_en: “European” starts with the consonant sound /yoo/, so “a” is correct despite the initial vowel letter.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She is very good ______ mathematics.
questions.explanation_en: The fixed phrase is “good at” a subject or skill.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The teacher congratulated him ______ his success.
questions.explanation_en: The verb “congratulate” takes “on” with the achievement: congratulated him on his success.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She is married ______ a doctor.
questions.explanation_en: “Married to” a person is the correct collocation.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: She is suffering ______ high fever.
questions.explanation_en: We suffer from a disease or illness, so “suffering from” is used.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The Principal was annoyed ______ the students for coming late.
questions.explanation_en: “Annoyed with” is used for a person (annoyed at/about a thing).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Divide the sweets ______ the three children equally.
questions.explanation_en: “Among” is used for more than two persons or things; “between” is for two.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Aman is senior ______ me by two years.
questions.explanation_en: Words such as senior, junior, superior, inferior, prefer take “to”, not “than”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The old man was accused ______ theft.
questions.explanation_en: “Accuse” is followed by “of”: accused of theft.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: I prefer tea ______ coffee.
questions.explanation_en: “Prefer” is always followed by “to”, never “than”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Beware ______ pickpockets in crowded places.
questions.explanation_en: The verb “beware” takes “of”: Beware of pickpockets.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Neither the manager nor the employees ______ present in the meeting.
questions.explanation_en: In “neither...nor”, the verb agrees with the noun nearest to it. “Employees” is plural, so “were”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Each of the boys ______ given a prize.
questions.explanation_en: “Each” is singular and takes a singular verb, even when followed by “of + plural noun”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Mathematics ______ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation_en: Subjects ending in -ics (mathematics, physics, economics) are treated as singular.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The number of applicants ______ increasing every year.
questions.explanation_en: “The number of” is singular (the number is increasing); “a number of” would be plural.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Either of the two answers ______ correct.
questions.explanation_en: “Either” means one of the two and is singular, so it takes “is”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Bread and butter ______ my usual breakfast.
questions.explanation_en: Two nouns that form one idea (bread and butter, rice and curry) take a singular verb.

tests.description: 35 most expected questions on Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration, with solutions.

tests.title: English Language & Comprehension Practice — Grammar (Part 2)
tests.subject: Computer Science
tests.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Ten kilometres ______ a long distance to walk.
questions.explanation_en: A plural expression of distance, money, time or weight used as a single unit takes a singular verb.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The Principal as well as the teachers ______ invited to the function.
questions.explanation_en: With “as well as”, “along with”, “together with”, the verb agrees with the first subject (Principal – singular).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Many a student ______ failed in this test.
questions.explanation_en: “Many a” is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: Many a student has failed.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: The police ______ investigating the case.
questions.explanation_en: “Police” is a collective noun that is always plural in usage, so it takes a plural verb.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘The police arrested the thief.’

options.en: The thief was arrested by the police.
The thief is arrested by the police.
The thief had been arrested by the police.
The police was arrested by the thief.

questions.explanation_en: Simple past active becomes was/were + V3 in the passive; the object becomes the subject.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘The students completed the project.’

options.en: The project is completed by the students.
The project has been completed by the students.
The project was completed by the students.
The students were completed by the project.

questions.explanation_en: Simple past: object + was/were + V3 + by + agent.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘Who wrote this letter?’

options.en: By whom is this letter written?
By whom has this letter been written?
By whom was this letter written?

questions.explanation_en: For a 'Who' question in the active voice, the passive begins 'By whom', and the tense is kept: simple past 'wrote' becomes 'was written'. 'Has been written' changes the tense.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘She is writing a novel.’

options.en: A novel is being written by her.
A novel is written by her.
A novel was being written by her.
A novel has been written by her.

questions.explanation_en: Present continuous passive = is/am/are + being + V3.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘They will have finished the work by noon.’

options.en: The work will be finished by them by noon.
The work will have been finished by them by noon.
The work would have been finished by them by noon.
The work has been finished by them by noon.

questions.explanation_en: Future perfect passive = will have been + V3.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘Someone has stolen my bicycle.’

options.en: My bicycle was stolen by someone.

questions.explanation_en: Present perfect passive = has/have been + V3; the vague agent ‘someone’ is normally omitted.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change the voice: ‘Do it at once.’

options.en: Let it be done at once.

questions.explanation_en: Imperative sentences become passive with ‘Let + object + be + V3’.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into the active voice: ‘The window was broken by the boy.’

options.en: The boy has broken the window.
The boy was breaking the window.

questions.explanation_en: Simple past passive (was broken) becomes simple past active (broke).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into the active voice: ‘A letter was being written by Neha.’
questions.explanation_en: Past continuous passive (was being written) corresponds to past continuous active (was writing).

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: He said, “I am happy.”

options.en: He said that he was happy.
He said that he is happy.
He said that I was happy.
He said that he had been happy.

questions.explanation_en: Present simple becomes past simple in reported speech when the reporting verb is in the past; pronoun I changes to he.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, “Where do you live?”

options.en: She asked me where I lived.
She told me where did I live.
She asked me where do you live.
She asked me that where I lived.

questions.explanation_en: A wh-question is reported with ‘asked’, statement word order and no ‘that’.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said, “The earth moves round the sun.”

options.en: The teacher said that the earth moved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had moved round the sun.
The teacher told that the earth moves round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun.

questions.explanation_en: A universal truth does not change tense in indirect speech.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, “Please help me.”

options.en: He ordered her to help him.
He requested her to help him.
He said her to help me.
He asked that she helps him.

questions.explanation_en: A polite request with ‘please’ is reported with ‘requested’ + to-infinitive.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: “Alas! I have failed,” said the boy.

options.en: The boy said that alas he has failed.
The boy exclaimed that I had failed.
The boy exclaimed sorrowfully that he had failed.
The boy asked sorrowfully whether he had failed.

questions.explanation_en: Exclamations are reported with ‘exclaimed with joy/sorrow’; present perfect shifts to past perfect.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into direct speech: He asked me if I had finished my work.

options.en: He said to me, “Have you finished my work?”
He said to me, “Had I finished my work?”
He said to me, “Have you finished your work?”
He said to me, “Have I finished your work?”

questions.explanation_en: The 'if' clause shows a yes/no question; the past perfect in the report goes back to the present perfect, and the pronouns change I → you and my → your: “Have you finished your work?”.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: She said, “I will come tomorrow.”

options.en: She said that she would come the next day.
She said that she will come tomorrow.
She said that I would come tomorrow.
She said that she would come tomorrow.

questions.explanation_en: Will becomes would and tomorrow becomes the next day / the following day.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en: Change into indirect speech: The captain said to the team, “Let us play carefully.”

options.en: The captain said to the team that let us play carefully.
The captain proposed to the team that they should play carefully.
The captain ordered the team to play carefully.
The captain asked the team that we play carefully.

questions.explanation_en: ‘Let us’ expresses a suggestion and is reported with ‘proposed/suggested that ... should’.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate question tag for the blank.
Let's go for a walk after dinner, ______?
questions.explanation_en: A sentence beginning with 'Let's' (a suggestion that includes the speaker) always takes the tag 'shall we?'. 'Will we' and 'don't we' do not fit a suggestion.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Choose the most appropriate question tag for the blank.
Nobody called me while I was out, ______?
questions.explanation_en: 'Nobody' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive; indefinite pronouns like nobody, everyone and someone are picked up by 'they'. Hence 'did they?'.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
______ he worked very hard, he could not clear the examination.
questions.explanation_en: The two clauses contrast (hard work, yet failure), so a concessive conjunction is needed: 'Although'. 'Because' shows cause, 'unless' a condition and 'whether' a choice.

questions.chapter: English Language & Comprehension — Grammar: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions, Agreement, Voice & Narration
questions.question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The roses in your garden smell ______.
questions.explanation_en: 'Smell' here is a linking verb (like look, feel, taste, seem), so it is followed by an adjective describing the subject: 'smell sweet'. An adverb is used only with an action verb, e.g. 'He chewed slowly'.
